Anthropic’s network and Congress

452 of 533

members of Congress have a tie on the public record to Anthropic’s network: 333 through something the network or the member did, 119 only through what third parties did. The network is the company, the funders behind it, the groups they fund, and their PACs and lobbyists.

Each dot is one of the 533 members serving on Nov. 26, 2026. A tie is a public record that links the member and the network: a contribution, a lobbying report on the member’s bill, a fellow in the office, a statement.

The network, by one chain: Coefficient Giving (then Open Philanthropy) named Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna as its main funders; it awarded Georgetown’s CSET $55.0M in 2019; 19 committee appearances by CSET’s witnesses are on record here. Third parties are lobbyists at the network’s lobbying firms, who gave their own money, and super PACs that received network money and made their own expenditures. A tie can cut either way: a statement may be criticism, and a super PAC may have spent against the member. It is not an allegation, and a contribution is not a vote.

Start with the company: its employees’ own gifts, and its PAC’s.

What counts as a tie: the eleven kinds of record

A tie is one or more public records that link a member now serving and the network. Each count is the members with at least one record of that kind.

I · The arrival

At the end of 2024, 10 members now serving had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. By Sept. 30, 2026: 196.

The employees gave their own money: $5.6M, 92% of it dated 2026. The company’s PAC made its first gift on record to a member now serving on June 29, 2026; by Sept. 30 it had given $200K to 81 members, 18 of whom had no gift from an employee.

Source: FEC contribution records in this project’s tables: contributions to the campaign, leadership PAC or single-member joint fundraising committee of a serving member, through Sept. 30, 2026; ANTHROPAC is Anthropic PBC’s political action committee.

A person’s contribution is their own money, not their employer’s. Employer is as the giver reported it to the FEC. Both counts are of the members serving on Nov. 26, 2026; the record stops at Sept. 30, 2026.

$5.8M in all. The large money moved another way.

Every gift on record to a member now serving (1,027 from Anthropic’s employees, 87 from its PAC), who gave, and where it landed

Through Sept. 30, 2026. The first chart’s scale is logarithmic: each line is ten times the one below; dots are translucent, so a bright patch is many gifts of one size on nearby dates. Givers are not named here; two people who share a first name and a surname count as one. A total is what the committees received, not what a member asked for. Among the largest recipients, Republicans are more than half of the five largest and of every longer list up to fourteen.

II · The bigger money

Anthropic announced $40.0M for Public First Action. There the trail stops: no filing in this record lists the group’s donors.

FEC receipts show Public First Action gave to 6 committees. The largest candidate total was $15.0M for Alexander Bores, outside Congress, while the committees reported $2.2M against sitting member Seth Moulton.

Sources include Anthropic’s announcements and FEC receipt and outside-spending filings.

This record traces no contribution to a specific expenditure. A contribution does not direct spending.

The network’s funders gave more, and for longer.

What the recipient committees reported

FEC filings record $30.3M from Public First Action to 6 committees. They separately record $32.9M in designated independent spending by those committees. $6.7M for or against 7 members now serving.

II · The bigger money

The network’s funders gave more: $170M to outside political groups since 2016, $100M of it from Dustin Moskovitz to Future Forward.

The spending panel covers committees with a network receipt on file and spending that names a serving member.

Sources include FEC contribution and outside-spending reports, BEMC 4 Association’s IRS filing and Anthropic’s announcements.

This record traces no gift to a specific expenditure.

One kind of money reaches more members than any of this, and the network did not give it.

What the 25 committees spent, and what the network gave them

II · The bigger money

Lobbyists’ own gifts reach the most members: $1.8M went to campaigns or committees linked to 356 serving members.

Counted: a gift whose giver was a registered lobbyist at a firm that had a network client in that period. Each lit seat has a campaign or committee linked to a gift.

Lobbyists’ semi-annual contribution reports to Congress, Feb. 19, 2021 to June 30, 2026. Filed recipient names, and committee records where the filing gives them, identify the member for each counted gift.

The gift is the lobbyist’s own money. The record does not say why it was made. Named lobbyists only: $1.3M in 1,022 gifts.

That is the lobbyists’ own money. Anthropic’s lobbying is on another record.

Lobbyists’ personal gifts by election cycle

118 lobbyists at 23 firms made 1,492 gifts linked to 164 Democrats, 191 Republicans and 1 independent. The total has grown in each cycle; for 2026, the reports read so far stop at June 30.

III · The lobbying

Anthropic reported $5.6M in lobbying expenses from January through September 2026.

The company began filing its own expenses in 2024. Outside firms filed the earliest reports in this record.

Source: quarterly federal lobbying reports (LD-2) filed by or for Anthropic through Sept. 30, 2026.

Amounts are as filed, rounded. In quarters with a company report, the totals use its expenses alone.

Which bills did its reports name?

The network’s share of 2025 filing totals

The comparison uses federal lobbying reports that name AI or an AI bill by title, as classified in the pack’s filing census. Filings can cover several issues and give one dollar total for all of them.

III · The lobbying

The three bill families most often named in lobbying reports filed for Anthropic are about chips.

All six sponsors received gifts from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. How often did a sponsor in the reports receive a gift?

Sources: quarterly lobbying reports through Sept. 30, 2026, verified sponsors of stand-alone bills and federal contribution filings.

A report naming a bill leaves open whether the sponsor’s office was contacted. No filing in this record ties a gift to a bill.

The gifts and the lobbying are recent. Who was Congress hearing from before them?

The bills and the sponsors on record

The bill titles are excerpts from the official titles as introduced. Sponsor lists cover members now serving. Campaign gifts are counted across all years on record.

IV · The decade before

By the end of 2024, seven of the network’s funders had awarded $528M in grants, and Congress had heard from seven of their grantees.

By then, ten of the members now serving had received money from Anthropic’s employees or its PAC. The grants supported work on AI, technology, biosecurity and catastrophic risk; none of the grants shown names a member of Congress as its recipient.

Source: IRS Form 990 grant schedules and the funders’ own published grant lists; witness lists from congress.gov, House committee pages and Senate hearing transcripts.

A grant to an organisation is not money to a member, and an award is not a payment on its date. Testifying is not lobbying.

Witnesses visit. Who works inside?

The 63 appearances, the grants by year and the 10 largest grantees

Each appearance is at a committee’s invitation. Testifying is not lobbying, and nothing in this record ties a grant to an appearance or to a person.

IV · The decade before

Horizon, a network grantee, has funded 25 fellows inside Congress.

The Horizon Institute for Public Service has $11.9M in network grants on record. Horizon says the host manages a fellow’s work.

Each dot is one person.

Source: Horizon Institute placement pages and alumni lists, and its “Host a Fellow” page as saved in 2026; House and Senate payroll reports, lobbyists’ disclosed former posts and organisations’ staff pages; IRS Form 990 grant schedules; for the sheet, FEC contribution records through Sept. 30, 2026.

Horizon also has funders outside the network. A job or a seat is not evidence about the work done in it.

Grants, hearings, fellows, jobs, money. What does that leave on file for each member?

The 20 hosts of Horizon’s fellows, and where the 64 went

Hosts as the programme’s roster lists them, with the year each placement began. Fellows and former staff are counted, not named.

V · The sum

A record of ties, not a record of influence.

240 of the 452 members with a tie have one or two kinds of record. The opening slide’s two members again, with what is on file for each: seven kinds of record for Ted Lieu, one for Thom Tillis.

Each dot is one of the 533 members serving on Nov. 26, 2026, by party; records through Sept. 30, 2026.

What is on file for all 533 members, and how it was counted

Records through Sept. 30, 2026; independent audits of the latest update were still open on Nov. 26, 2026. The 29 source figures, the tables and the method are in the repository.
